idiom_name: middleware chain of functions: app.use((req, res, next) => ...) / axios interceptors
implementation_notes: In JavaScript the pattern degenerates into an array of functions, so the classic Interceptor/Dispatcher classes are replaced by function composition: the framework's use()/compose() walks the array, hands each function (req, res, next) as the context, and calling next() continues the chain while returning early - or calling next('route') to skip the current stack - vetoes the rest. Client-side calls follow the same shape with a dedicated registry: axios.interceptors.request.use / response.use register and return a handle, and eject()/clear() exist because registrations otherwise live for the process lifetime. Only a library that must expose a version-stable extension contract across implementations still needs an explicit dispatcher object.
pitfalls: Forgetting to call next() (or next(err)) leaves the request hanging until the client times out - the most common middleware defect, and it fails silently in the logs.

Registration is process-lifetime state: adding an interceptor inside a request handler accumulates duplicates until the event emitter or axios registry explodes; keep the registration handle and eject it.

Order is insertion order, and error-handling middleware is distinguished only by arity ((err, req, res, next)) and must be registered last - reordering or wrapping an error middleware in an arrow with the wrong arity silently changes semantics.
Mounted middleware (app.use('/api', ...)) only runs for matching prefixes, so a global concern registered after a router never sees the responses handled before it.
